title: IB Maths AI Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
summary: IB Maths AI common mistakes can cost easy marks. Learn to read command terms, show evidence, add units, round correctly, and manage your exam time better.
body_markdown:
**IB Maths AI common mistakes** often involve reading, communication, accuracy, and timing rather than missing mathematical knowledge. You can prevent many of them by checking command terms, showing your method, adding units, keeping calculator precision, and pacing your work against the marks available.


Imagine a student finding the correct volume but forgetting cubic units, then calculating a correlation coefficient without interpreting it. The mathematics is mostly there. The answer is unfinished. These small gaps deserve focused practice because knowing a method and communicating it under pressure are different skills.


### The quick mistake checklist


Before moving on, check five things:


- Have I answered the command term?
- Have I shown enough mathematical evidence?
- Does my answer need units or context?
- Have I followed the accuracy requirement?
- Is my time proportional to the available marks?


Use this checklist during practice until it becomes familiar enough to apply in an exam.


### Misreading command terms


Command terms tell you what response the examiner expects. **Write down** usually calls for a direct answer with little or no calculation. **Show that** requires a logical route to the supplied result. **Interpret** asks what a result means in the situation. **Justify** requires supporting evidence.


Before calculating, underline the command term and translate it into an action. For **hence** , look back at the preceding result. For **interpret** , identify the variables you need to discuss. For **show that** , make sure your reasoning actually establishes the supplied answer.


Then check the marks. A one-mark prompt rarely needs half a page, while a multi-mark justification probably needs more than calculator output.


Practise this distinction using the[IB Maths AI Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-math-ai/questionbank) . After each attempt, check whether your response performed the requested action as well as producing the correct number.


### Giving an answer without enough evidence


A calculator can produce a regression model, probability, or intersection quickly. Your response must still communicate the mathematical method.


Visible working can support method marks when a final answer is incorrect, depending on the question and markscheme. A bare decimal gives little evidence of your approach, especially when one incorrect data entry changes the output.


Record the bridge between the question and your result: an equation, probability statement, substitution, model, or statistical test. You do not need every button press.


For example, writing only 0.0320.032


0.032


after a hypothesis test leaves its meaning unclear. Identify it as the p-value, compare it with the significance level, and state the contextual conclusion. Include hypotheses when required.


This is where[interpretation in IB Maths](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/why-does-ib-care-about-interpretation-more-than-precision-in-maths) becomes essential: the calculation supplies information, and your explanation answers the question.


### Forgetting units, labels, or context


A student carrying mathematics while a suitcase of forgotten units circles an airport carousel


*A student leaves a small but essential item behind.*


Writing 216216


216


instead of 216 cm3216\\text{ cm}^3


216


cm


3


can leave a volume answer incomplete. After calculating, ask what quantity you found, which unit belongs to it, and whether the value makes sense.


Length, area, and volume require different dimensions. Rates need both components, such as kilometres per hour. Money and counts may require contextual rounding, so a calculator's decimal display is not automatically a suitable final answer.


For graphs, provide appropriate labels and scales where required. For statistics, name the variables rather than concluding only that “there is a relationship.” Consult the[IB Maths AI Study Notes and practice resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-math-ai) when you can perform a procedure but struggle to explain its meaning.


### Rounding too early or incorrectly


Suppose an intermediate value is 2.674912.67491


2.67491


. Replacing it immediately with 2.672.67


2.67


and using that rounded number in later calculations introduces avoidable error. Through several stages, that difference can affect the final answer.


Keep full calculator precision and round at the end unless instructed otherwise. Store intermediate results rather than retyping shortened versions. Follow any accuracy instruction in the question and the general directions printed on your examination paper.


Before finishing, check whether the answer requires significant figures, decimal places, exact form, or a whole-number interpretation.


The[Math AI self-study resource guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-math-ai-sl-resources-self-study) can help structure targeted practice. Use RevisionDojo's Grading tools to review written responses, then check feedback against the solution and markscheme.


### Losing control of exam timing


Trying to perfect an early answer can leave later questions untouched. Use roughly one minute per mark as an initial pacing guide, adjusting it to the paper's stated duration and total marks. Some questions will take less time; others need more reading or interpretation.


Practise two passes. First, answer questions you can start confidently. If you become stuck, leave useful working, mark the question, and continue. Return with the remaining time, keeping a final buffer for missed parts, units, and accuracy.


Build timed practice with the[RevisionDojo Exam Builder](https://www.revisiondojo.com/test-builder?subject=289) . The[IB Math AI mock exam preparation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-math-ai-mock-exam-prep-november) can help you review each attempt and identify where time disappeared.


### Turn each lost mark into a rule


Keep a short mistake log. Replace “careless” with “ignored interpret,” “rounded an intermediate value,” or “omitted cubic units.” Add one prevention rule beside each error, then test it on similar questions.
